task_row_model.query: For f(x) = x^3 - 3x + 2, find all local extrema and classify each as a local minimum or maximum (give locations and types).

documents.content: A brief explanatory column on cubic polynomials: consider the cubic f(x) = x^3 - 3x + 2. Cubics typically have one or two turning points; this specific polynomial combines a leading x^3 term with a linear term of coefficient -3 and a constant shift of +2. Graphical commentary notes inflection behavior and how the linear coefficient translates the slope near the origin, but no derivative is computed here.

Textbook excerpt: differentiation rules and the second derivative test. The power rule: d/dx[x^n] = n x^{n-1}; derivatives are linear and constants vanish. A critical point is where f'(x)=0 or undefined. Second derivative test: if f'(c)=0 and f''(c)>0 then f has a local minimum at c; if f''(c)<0 then f has a local maximum at c. The test is local and assumes f is twice differentiable at c.

Handwritten-style solution notes: apply the power rule to f(x)=x^3-3x+2. Differentiating termwise gives f'(x)=3x^2-3. Set 3x^2-3=0 ⇒ x^2=1 ⇒ x=±1 (critical points). Differentiate again to get f''(x)=6x. Evaluate: f''(1)=6 and f''(-1)=-6. Also evaluate the original polynomial at these points: f(1)=1-3+2=0 and f(-1)=-1+3+2=4. These computations verify locations and curvature signs.

Reference note on cubic history and adjacent terminology: historically cubics were solved by Cardano in the 16th century; current computational practice often records counts of stationary points across sample polynomials. A short case study collected 243 random cubics and reported that about 68% had two stationary points by coefficient distribution, but these statistics and the historical asides are tangential to local-test computations.

task_row_model.golden_answer: For f(x)=x^3-3x+2, f'(x)=3x^2-3 so critical points satisfy 3x^2-3=0 ⇒ x=±1. The second derivative f''(x)=6x gives f''(1)=6>0, so a local minimum at x=1 (f(1)=0), and f''(-1)=-6<0, so a local maximum at x=-1 (f(-1)=4).
